topics.title: TCP congestion control
topics.source_text:
## The congestion window
TCP limits how much unacknowledged data a sender may have in flight with two windows. The receive window is advertised by the receiver and protects its buffer, while the congestion window is kept by the sender and protects the network. At any time the sender may transmit at most the minimum of the two windows. The congestion window is measured in bytes or in maximum segment sizes and changes as the sender learns about the state of the path.

## Slow start
A new connection, or a connection that has just recovered from a timeout, starts in slow start with a small congestion window of a few segments. In slow start the sender increases the congestion window by one maximum segment size for every acknowledgement it receives. Because every acknowledged segment enlarges the window, the congestion window roughly doubles in every round-trip time, which is exponential growth despite the name. Slow start ends when the congestion window reaches the slow start threshold, called ssthresh, or when a loss is detected.

## Congestion avoidance
Above the slow start threshold the sender switches to congestion avoidance, where the congestion window grows by about one maximum segment size per round-trip time. This linear growth probes for additional bandwidth carefully, because the sender is now close to the capacity at which losses occurred before. The combination of this additive increase with the multiplicative decrease after a loss is called AIMD and produces the sawtooth shape of the congestion window over time.

## Loss detection
TCP treats a lost segment as a signal of congestion, and it detects losses in two ways. If no acknowledgement arrives before the retransmission timeout expires, the sender assumes heavy congestion, sets ssthresh to half of the data in flight and restarts slow start from a window of one segment. If the receiver gets segments out of order, it repeats the acknowledgement of the last in-order byte, and these duplicate acknowledgements tell the sender that later segments are still arriving.

## Fast retransmit and fast recovery
After three duplicate acknowledgements the sender retransmits the missing segment immediately instead of waiting for the retransmission timer, which is called fast retransmit. Fast recovery then sets ssthresh to half of the data in flight and continues with a congestion window of about that size instead of falling back to slow start. Because the duplicate acknowledgements prove that the network still delivers segments, this milder reaction keeps the throughput higher than a timeout would.

topics.title: REST-style HTTP APIs
topics.source_text:
## Resources and representations
In a REST-style HTTP API every important concept, such as an order or a list of orders, is a resource identified by a URI. Clients never receive the internal object or database row itself, only a representation of the resource, for example a JSON document. The Content-Type header tells the client how to interpret the representation, and the same resource can be offered in several formats. Each request carries all the information needed to process it, so the server does not depend on a hidden conversation state between requests.

## Methods, safety and idempotency
The HTTP method expresses the intent of a request. GET only reads a resource and is safe, which means browsers, caches and proxies may repeat or prefetch it without changing anything on the server. PUT replaces a resource and DELETE removes it, and both are idempotent, so sending the same request several times has the same effect as sending it once. POST asks the server to process the enclosed data, is neither safe nor idempotent, and therefore must not be retried blindly after a timeout.

## Status codes and errors
The status code tells the client the class of the outcome without parsing the body. The code 201 Created confirms that a new resource was made, 400 reports invalid input, 404 reports a missing resource and 409 reports a conflict with the current state. A 429 response asks the client to slow down, and a 503 response reports temporary overload, ideally together with a Retry-After header. Problem details in the application/problem+json format describe an error in a machine-readable way, so clients can react to a stable error type instead of the human-readable text.

## Caching and concurrency
An ETag identifies one version of a representation. A client that already holds a version sends it in the If-None-Match header, and the server answers 304 Not Modified when nothing has changed, which saves bandwidth. The same validator protects against lost updates, because a write sent with If-Match only succeeds if the resource still has that version. Otherwise the server answers 412 Precondition Failed, and the client must read the new state before deciding again.

## Long-running operations
An operation that takes longer than a normal request should not keep the connection waiting. The server can answer 202 Accepted, which means the request was accepted but not yet completed, together with a link to a status resource. The client then follows the progress of the operation by polling that resource or by subscribing to notifications, and it reads the final result when the status shows completion.

topics.title: Linear time-invariant systems and stability
topics.source_text:
## Linearity and time invariance
A system is linear if it satisfies superposition, which means the response to a weighted sum of inputs equals the same weighted sum of the individual responses. A system is time-invariant if delaying the input only delays the output by the same amount without changing its shape. Systems with both properties are called linear time-invariant systems, and they can be analysed with a common set of tools in the time domain and in the frequency domain.

## Impulse response and convolution
The impulse response is the output of the system when the input is a unit impulse. For a linear time-invariant system the impulse response describes the system completely, because every input signal can be written as a sum of scaled and shifted impulses. The output for an arbitrary input is therefore the convolution of the input with the impulse response. A system is causal if its impulse response is zero for negative time, so the output never depends on future inputs.

## Transfer function
The Laplace transform turns convolution in the time domain into multiplication in the complex frequency domain. The transfer function is the ratio of the Laplace transform of the output to the Laplace transform of the input when all initial conditions are zero. It equals the Laplace transform of the impulse response, and for systems described by linear differential equations it is a ratio of two polynomials in s. Evaluating the transfer function on the imaginary axis gives the frequency response, which shows the gain and the phase shift at each frequency.

## Poles, zeros and stability
The roots of the numerator polynomial of the transfer function are the zeros, and the roots of the denominator polynomial are the poles. A continuous-time system is bounded-input bounded-output stable if every bounded input produces a bounded output. For a causal linear time-invariant system this holds exactly when all poles lie strictly in the left half of the complex plane. A pole on the imaginary axis gives a sustained oscillation or a constant response, and a pole in the right half-plane gives a response that grows without bound.

## Feedback
In a closed-loop system the output is measured and fed back to be compared with the reference signal, and the controller acts on the difference, which is called the error. With negative feedback, a forward transfer function G(s) and a feedback path H(s), the closed-loop transfer function is G(s) divided by one plus G(s)H(s). Feedback can reduce the sensitivity of the system to parameter changes and to disturbances, but a high loop gain can move the closed-loop poles towards the right half-plane and make the system unstable.
